prize_parts.citation: for showing how collateral constraints and asset prices amplify and propagate shocks into persistent credit cycles

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single part for B040 with Kiyotaki and Moore. The round-1 exchange sharpened my reasons but did not reverse them. Kiyotaki and Moore (1997) identify one general mechanism. Borrowing limits tied to collateral value feed back on asset prices, so small temporary shocks become large and persistent. It is a conceptual advance, nearly three decades old, and it is now a standard way to model financial frictions and crises. Its attribution is the cleanest on the shortlist, since the originating paper has two authors and no co-originator is missing. I would draft the citation around the mechanism and its influence on how credit cycles are modelled. It should not claim that the quantitative size of amplification is settled. The chair's questions ask which criterion I rank first. For me it is clean attribution combined with maturity, with conceptual generality third. On those three B040 is ahead of every other shortlisted candidate. I do not use the four-four split with B044 as evidence on merit, and I do not choose B040 because it has the most opening support. The balance is closer than my opening ranking implied. After the arguments from Krusell, Teorell, Fredriksson and Hjalmarsson, I now rate B044, narrowed to the trade-shock evidence with Autor, Dorn and Hanson, as a serious competitor. I have therefore replaced B036 with B044 among my alternatives, and B002 stays.
statement.case_against: The most serious reservation for B040 is, as a metascience researcher, the gap between influence and direct evidence. The mechanism has shaped models more than it has been tested, and its quantitative importance is still contested. A prize here would honour the theory more than tested evidence, and I think the Committee should say so openly. A second reservation is overlap with the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises, and with the financial-accelerator strand. That strand includes Gertler and Gilchrist, whose empirical work I leave out. I think the mechanism is distinct from the bank-run and deposit-insurance work, but I cannot verify the extent of the overlap beyond my own knowledge. The narrow two-person pairing rests essentially on one seminal paper and its extensions. If colleagues who know macro-finance better show that quantitative validation is weaker than I assume, B040 would lose ground to B044.

responses.point: Krusell moved from B002 to B044. He anchors the citation on the trade-shock evidence and credits Autor, Dorn and Hanson as the joint authors of the core papers. He says a decade of replication has refined the magnitudes without overturning the finding. He ranks B040 just behind B044 because its empirical test is indirect and the 2022 prize narrows its novelty.
responses.response: His anchoring of the citation on the trade-shock evidence, with Dorn included, is the strongest version of B044. It answers the attribution worry I raised in round 1, because that design is a three-author product. He is also right that a decade of replication across countries counts for more than recency alone. We differ on weights. As a replication researcher, I read the persistence of the shift-share inference debate as a limit on how precisely the policy-relevant magnitudes are known, not only as a refinement. I also put more weight on twenty-five-plus years of scrutiny, which B044 cannot yet match. On his point that B040's validation is indirect, I agree, and I list it as my main uncertainty. I read it as a reason for a carefully worded citation, not a reason to prefer an empirical design that has an unsettled magnitude debate of its own.

responses.point: Teorell moved from B017 to B044. He argues that the task framework and the trade-shock evidence share one labour-demand question and can sit in one citation, but he calls this a judgement and the main open issue. He lists B040 as an alternative because its attribution is cleaner.
responses.response: I appreciate that he labels the one-achievement reading a judgement and not a fact. That is my sticking point with B044. If the committee takes the narrow reading (trade-shock evidence only), attribution is clean and I would regard B044 as roughly level with B040 on that criterion. If it wants the wider technology-and-tasks citation, the lineage reaches Acemoglu, Katz, Levy and Murnane, and the three-name cap forces arbitrary cuts. I cannot judge from my own field which reading the literature supports, so I rely on his and Krusell's assessments. B040 does not depend on that call. That robustness is part of why I keep it first. If the committee settles on the narrow reading, I would reconsider and would be comfortable with B044.

responses.point: The chair keeps B040 with Kiyotaki and Moore. He qualifies his opening wording: only Bernanke among the accelerator authors is a laureate, so excluding Gertler and Gilchrist should rest on the independent origin and distinctness of the collateral-constraint mechanism, not on prior recognition. He also declines to add Autor as a second part.
responses.response: I agree with his correction and am adopting it. My round-1 phrasing implied that the 2022 prize and the accelerator strand were separate topics, and the sounder argument is the independent origin of the mechanism. I also agree with him that a one-name second part for Autor would split credit for the China-shock work and misdescribe it. That answers the chair's question about multi-part configurations: I see no coherent two-part configuration with B040 and one name from B044. I would not add Gertler as a third name for the empirical strand either. That would blur the origin of the mechanism, and the cost I flagged (honouring theory over tested evidence) is better stated in the citation and in the discussion than fixed by widening the credit. His position is also the one most exposed to the chair's own field-proximity flag, so I do not count his preference as independent support for B040 and base my case on my own reading.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson ranks B044 first and notes the China-shock design is transparent and replicated. She argues it rests on direct identification, whereas validation of the collateral-constraint mechanism is more indirect. She also dropped Katz and now names Autor, Dorn and Hanson.
responses.response: Her argument about direct identification is the best case against my position, and I accept its premise about B040's indirect validation. I disagree about how much that should decide the question. A prize should reward what changed the field and how well the contribution has lasted, and a mechanism that organised a generation of macro-finance models and crisis analysis has a record that the trade-shock papers cannot yet match. I welcome her move to Autor, Dorn and Hanson, because it removes my worry about a three-author design being split. My remaining difference is on maturity and the unresolved question of magnitudes. She has shifted me toward treating B044 as a close alternative and not a distant one.

uncertainties: How much of the collateral-constraint amplification territory the 2022 prize and Bernanke's earlier recognition already cover, and whether that lowers the marginal case. I rely on colleagues' descriptions and my own general knowledge.
How well the quantitative implications of collateral constraints have been validated independently of the theory. A weaker record than I assume would favour B044.

Whether the Committee reads B044 narrowly (trade-shock evidence, with Autor, Dorn and Hanson) or broadly (with tasks and skill bias). On the narrow reading I would regard it as roughly level with B040 on attribution.
How much the persisting shift-share inference and magnitude debate should count against B044 relative to the indirect validation of B040.
Whether excluding Gertler and Gilchrist makes a B040 award honour theory over tested evidence, and whether the citation can say so without understating the mechanism's influence.
I rely on general knowledge and the supplied round-1 files, not independent verification of citation counts, replication records or attribution.
statement.conflict_note: No change from round 1. The supplied profile shows no co-authorship, institutional or collaborative tie to Kiyotaki, Moore or the credited names on my alternatives B044 (Autor, Dorn, Hanson, Katz) and B002 (Chetty, Hendren, Friedman). My listed co-authors and networks (Camerer, Pfeiffer, Holzmeister, Huber, Nosek, Rand, Fudenberg, Nowak, Ellingsen, Johannesson, Almenberg, Brodeur) are in behavioural, experimental and metascience research, and none is credited on the shortlist. I note that Ellingsen, a former chair and my SSE co-author, also co-authored with Friberg, and that Johannesson, my main co-author, is a former committee member. Neither is a candidate. My metascience orientation may make me more cautious about theory-led evidence and more receptive to replicated empirical designs, and I have tried to apply the common criteria despite it. These disclosures are not adjudicated.
